strengths: NC-OOD is a simple, interpretable post-hoc detector with practical value. Using classifier weights and a global feature mean avoids storing a nearest-neighbor feature bank or fitting a covariance model, with little additional computation after classification.

The evaluation meaningfully spans CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, ImageNet, two CNN families, and cross-entropy and supervised contrastive training. Table 1 reports average AUROC improvements from 94.92 to 95.36 on CIFAR-10 and from 93.40 to 94.15 on ImageNet over the strongest listed baselines. Under contrastive training, average FPR95 improves from 11.61 to 9.84.

The component ablation provides convincing evidence of complementarity on ImageNet: Table 4 reports 88.69 AUROC for pScore, 87.08 for feature L1 norm, and 94.15 for their combination. This supports the combined detector beyond its geometric illustration.

The scoring equations are straightforward to implement. The manuscript supplies per-dataset results, both AUROC and FPR95, training details, and the hyperparameter search grid. Selecting alpha using Gaussian-noise validation avoids explicitly tuning against the evaluated natural OOD datasets.
weaknesses: Theorem 1 is stronger than its proof establishes. Equation (3) concerns normalized alignment, whereas Equation (1) asserts convergence of unnormalized vectors; multiplying a vanishing angular error by an unbounded class-mean norm need not yield a vanishing residual. Equation (2) also requires control of the denominator. Appropriate scale assumptions or a revised directional statement are needed. Furthermore, the experiments do not measure whether collapse strength explains detection performance in the evaluated checkpoints.

The distinctive contribution is insufficiently isolated. Appendix B acknowledges that CSI already combines cosine similarity with feature magnitude, while pScore can be written as a centered class logit divided by centered feature length. A matched comparison replacing classifier weights with centered empirical class means would directly test the proposed weight-prototype advantage. Comparisons with closely related approaches such as MaxLogit and ViM are also absent, leaving the incremental benefit incompletely established.

The claim of consistently superior generalizability exceeds the results. On DenseNet/CIFAR-100, Table 10 reports NC-OOD FPR95 of 62.62 versus 47.36 for KNN, a substantial operating-point disadvantage. Table 3 also shows lower average AUROC than the best baseline for both DenseNet settings. Meanwhile, the contrastive AUROC improvement is only 0.15 points, without uncertainty estimates or repeated-training results. These findings support useful competitiveness but qualify the stronger robustness claims.

The filtering-norm ablation does not cleanly distinguish norm geometry from effective filtering strength. Table 6 uses alpha = 0.001 for norms with substantially different magnitudes, and Table 13 assigns L1 a larger coefficient than the alternatives. Although Gaussian-noise tuning is described, the absence of sensitivity curves or scale-matched comparisons limits the conclusion that L1 itself is responsible for the advantage.

There is a material reporting inconsistency: the six ReAct+DICE FPR95 entries in Table 10 average approximately 45.00, whereas the reported average is 76.45, reversing its comparison with NC-OOD. Reproduction from the manuscript is also limited by unspecified KNN neighborhood size and supervised-contrastive classifier-head training details; claimed speed advantages lack measurements. Incorrect table references are minor presentation issues. Overall, the efficient design and demonstrated gains balance against the theoretical and contribution-attribution gaps, placing the manuscript near the acceptance boundary.
